in a large cohort of HIV-positive patients coinfected with tuberculosis, the response to antiretoviral therapy was similar regardless of whether the patient was receiving an efavirenz- or non-efavirnez-containing regimen, although response to treatment varied significantly across geographical locations.
the response to ART was variable across geographical regions, while the ART regimen (containing efavirenz, or not) had no impact on the proportion who were virological suppressed or died at 12 month.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are differences in response to antiviral therapy in HIV/TB patients being treated for TB in EE, WE, and LA.
the choice of ART regimen (efavirnez or non-efavirnez containing) does not appear to influence outcomes at 12 month follow up.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the response to antiretoviral therapy varied across geographical regions but the antiretrovirus regimen used did not influence the response to treatment.
the response to ART was better in Western Europe than in other regions.
there is no difference in outcomes in patients who received either an EFV or non-EFV based regimen.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of ART regimen does not appear to be the main driver of these differences.
the choice of antiretrovirus regimen is not as important as the quality of care in ensuring good outcomes for people with HIV/TB co-infection in low and middle-income countries.
